title: Overlap Measurement — Core Method
description: Two databases overlap when they hold the same records, and the Jaccard index — intersection over union of sampled identifiers — measures exactly how much. Sampling a few thousand IDs from each side gives a tight estimate without comparing billions of rows. High overlap with different schemas means the same facts dressed differently; high overlap with the same schema means a replica. Topology analysis starts here because overlap is the simplest structural relationship between databases. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
demo:
import random
random.seed(3)
A = set(random.sample(range(10000), 2000))
B = set(random.sample(range(10000), 2000))
B |= set(random.sample(sorted(A), 500))
j = len(A & B) / len(A | B)
print("estimated Jaccard overlap: %.3f" % j)

title: Reference Graph Construction — Core Method
description: Databases reference each other through foreign-key-like fields: a record in one holds the identifier of a record in another. The analyzer scans field names and value patterns for these cross-references and builds a directed graph of who points to whom. Edge weights count how many references were observed, so heavily-linked pairs stand out from incidental mentions. This graph is the raw material for every deeper topological question — dependencies, clusters, and hubs all derive from it. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
demo:
REFS = [("orders", "customers"), ("orders", "products"), ("reviews", "products"),
        ("reviews", "customers"), ("orders", "customers")]
from collections import Counter
edges = Counter(REFS)
for (u, v), n in edges.most_common():
    print("%s -> %s  (%d references)" % (u, v, n))

title: Dependency Edge Inference — Core Method
description: A reference becomes a dependency when one database cannot be understood — or rebuilt — without the other. The analyzer promotes reference edges to dependency edges using signals like reference density, nullability, and whether the referencing side stores a copy or only a pointer. Dependencies must form a coherent direction; contradictions flag modeling errors in the source schemas. The resulting dependency DAG tells operators which databases to back up, migrate, or rebuild first. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.

title: Containment Testing — Core Method
description: Sometimes one database is entirely contained in another — a filtered export, a materialized view, an older snapshot. Containment testing samples identifiers from the smaller side and checks their presence in the larger; if every sample hits, containment is likely, with confidence rising in the sample size. The test also records which fields differ, distinguishing a true subset from a lossy copy. Knowing containment lets the analyzer prune redundant databases from search plans entirely. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
demo:
import random
random.seed(11)
big = set(range(100000))
small = set(random.sample(sorted(big), 5000))
sample = random.sample(sorted(small), 500)
contained = all(x in big for x in sample)
print("sampled %d ids, all present: %s" % (len(sample), contained))

title: Topology Map Export — Core Method
description: The final product of topology analysis is a portable map: nodes for databases with their sizes and schemas, edges for references, overlaps, and dependencies, all serialized in a standard graph format. Downstream tools — visualizers, migration planners, search routers — consume this map instead of re-deriving the topology. The export includes the sampling parameters and confidence of every edge, so consumers know which relationships are measured and which are estimated. A fresh map is cut whenever the underlying databases change shape. At ladder rank 1 this is the simple core: a single, self-contained application of the method.
demo:
import json
topo = {"nodes": [{"db": "orders", "rows": 1200000}, {"db": "customers", "rows": 80000}],
        "edges": [{"from": "orders", "to": "customers", "kind": "reference", "n": 1190000}]}
doc = json.dumps(topo, indent=1)
print(doc[:200] + "...")
print("nodes:", len(topo["nodes"]), "edges:", len(topo["edges"]))
provenance: JAH Databases archive-intelligence tools program, lane T2a — public methods from established computer-science practice.
